newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW - Japan July current account data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Japan July current account data.

text.p: Japan's current account surplus fell 27.3 percent to 568.2 billion yen in July from a year ago, official data showed on Monday.
Economists polled by Reuters had forecast on average 495.5 billion yen surplus, down from 781.5 billion yen a year ago. Analysts' comments follow.
DAVID COHEN, ECONOMIST, MMS INTERNATIONAL TOKYO:

"It was actually slightly smaller decline than expected. It probably won't help the dollar at all right now. The dollar is probably getting more benefits at the moment from the expectations for a Fed rate hike at the September FOMC."
MASARU TAKAGI, CHIEF ECONOMIST, FUJI RESEARCH INSTITUTE:

"Today's result is one factor for a cheaper yen against the dollar. But recently, the balance of payments hasn't had a strong impact on the foreign exchange market. So today, the direction of interest rates between Japan and the U.S. is very, very important.

"I don't think so, yet (decline in surplus slowing). Still, the direction is a great improvement in trade of the Japanese current account balance. There is still a shift of production from Japan to overseas. At the same time, we have a huge inflow of foreign goods from Asian countries, the U.S. and others."

"This is a structural change, so I expect the situation to continue for sometime. If the Japanese yen is 100 to 110 yen against the dollar, I think there would be no strong, big change at all until the end of this year. So this downward trend in the surplus will continue for the time being."
SUSUMU TAKAHASHI, GENERAL MANAGER AT JAPAN RESEARCH INSTITUTE LTD:
"The current account surplus had fallen significantly in the past, but it won't fall in a monotonous way. The pace of shrinkage could slow down".
But given the the trend where export volume declines and import volume rises, the underlying trend of falling surplus should continue, he added.
